questions.q: How does this lesson's reproducibility argument for pinning differ from Chapter 1's stability argument?
options: There is no difference; they're the same argument
The stability argument protects future runs from silent breaks; the reproducibility argument says you need the exact dependency snapshot active at the time to reproduce a past numeric result at all
The reproducibility argument only applies to construction tests
The stability argument is about git, the reproducibility argument is about Python syntax
questions.explain: Chapter 1's pinning argument is forward-looking (avoid silent breaks going forward). This lesson adds a backward-looking argument: without the exact dependency snapshot from when a result was produced, you can't necessarily reproduce that specific numeric result later, even with the exact code.

questions.q: Why is pinning `qiskit==1.2.4` in pyproject.toml alone not sufficient for full reproducibility, according to the lesson?
options: It pins the direct dependency but not qiskit's own internal/transitive dependencies (like rustworkx or symengine), which can still resolve differently without a full lockfile
pyproject.toml files cannot specify exact versions
Because qiskit version numbers are not unique
Because pinning only works for Python 2
questions.explain: A top-level exact pin doesn't fix transitive dependency versions. A full lockfile (uv.lock, or a pip freeze snapshot) is needed to capture the entire resolved environment, not just the direct pin.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend naming a frozen dependency snapshot after the experiment tag (e.g. requirements-lock-exp-grover-10q-2026-10-18.txt)?
options: It's purely a stylistic preference with no functional benefit
It makes the connection between a specific result and its exact environment explicit and searchable, rather than implicit and easy to lose
Long filenames are required by pip
It prevents the lockfile from being committed to git
questions.explain: Tying the frozen snapshot's name to the experiment tag makes it immediately clear which locked environment corresponds to which reported result, rather than leaving that link to be remembered or reconstructed later.

questions.q: When a previously pinned SDK version becomes genuinely uninstallable later, what does the lesson say you should do?
options: Silently re-run on the closest available version and report the same old number as if nothing changed
Document that exact reproduction is no longer possible, re-run under the closest installable version, and report it as a new, separately tagged experiment
Delete the original result entirely since it can no longer be verified
Refuse to ever upgrade any dependency again
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against silently substituting a new result for an old one under the same label. Instead: document the limitation, re-run under a new version, and tag the new run separately -- any discrepancy is itself worth investigating, not discarding.

questions.q: In the six-month reproduction scenario, what does `git show exp-ghz-5q-2026-04-10:uv.lock` retrieve, and why does step 3 (uv sync) depend on it?
options: It retrieves the original author's name; step 3 doesn't depend on it

It retrieves the exact resolved dependency snapshot from the tagged commit, which uv sync uses to recreate the identical environment -- without it, the wrong environment could be reconstructed or reproduction becomes impossible
It retrieves the random seed used in the experiment
It retrieves the hardware calibration data from that date
questions.explain: The lockfile committed alongside the tag captures the exact dependency tree active at the time. Retrieving it via git show and recreating it with uv sync is what lets the environment -- not just the code -- be reconstructed faithfully.
